name: Remarket repossessed and returned equipment
summary: Equipment that customers return at the end of a lease, or that bailiffs seize after a default, sits in storage until the remarketing team sells it. A remarketing specialist reviews the condition report, an asset manager values the equipment, the specialist decides on repairs and picks a channel (an auction, the originating dealer, other dealers or a direct buyer), and the manager approves the plan and the minimum price. After the sale the specialist records the proceeds and costs, asks lease administration for the bill of sale and sends the results to recoveries when a defaulted balance remains. Waiting for inspections, repairs, auction dates and settlements makes the process slow, and storage charges and falling values mean every week of delay costs money.

baseline.org_archetype: A privately owned Canadian independent equipment lessor with about 55,000 active contracts and a ten-person asset management and remarketing team.
baseline.notes: Trucks, trailers, construction, agricultural, industrial, technology and medical equipment. Most small items go to online or site auctions; trucks and newer machinery often go to dealers.

trigger: Seized equipment arrives in storage after a repossession, or returned equipment's condition report is filed at the end of a lease.
end_state: The asset is sold and paid for, the proceeds and costs are recorded, the bill of sale is requested and, for seized equipment, the results are with recoveries.

volume.seasonality: Auction calendars are heavier in spring and fall; repossessions rose in 2020 after payment deferrals ended.

evidence.note: Organisation file range; about 70 off-lease returns and 45 repossessions a month feed it.

steps.name: Add the asset to the remarketing inventory
steps.description: When a bailiff confirms that seized equipment is in storage, or a returned asset's condition report is filed, the lease system changes the asset status to held for sale and puts it in the remarketing queue with the yard location and daily storage rate.

evidence.note: Status-driven queue in the lease system is an author estimate of common set-up.

steps.name: Review the asset file
steps.description: The remarketing specialist reads the bailiff report or return condition report, photos, serial numbers, hours or kilometres, the contract status and pool code, and for seized equipment the date the notice of intended disposition went out, and decides whether the condition information is good enough to price the asset.

error.defect_description: Notice date or a lien on another creditor's registration overlooked.

evidence.note: Branch share is an author estimate; bailiff reports for seized equipment are often thinner than return inspections.

steps.name: Order an inspection at the storage yard
steps.description: The asset logistics coordinator asks the yard or a field inspector for photos, an hour meter reading, a start-up and function check and a list of missing parts, and agrees the fee.

evidence.note: Author estimate.

steps.name: Yard or inspector reports the condition
steps.description: The yard or inspector visits the equipment and sends the condition report and photos, which are filed in imaging and attached to the asset record.

evidence.note: Author estimate of field inspection turnaround.

steps.name: Value the asset and suggest a channel
steps.description: An asset manager checks recent auction results, value guides and dealer listings for the same make, model, year and hours, estimates the auction value and the dealer or retail value net of transport, commission and repairs, and suggests a channel and reserve. High-value or specialised items get a third-party appraisal.

error.defect_description: Value set from poor comparables, so the reserve is too high or too low.

evidence.note: Valuation bases follow the sources; the appraisal share is an author estimate.

steps.name: Third-party appraiser values the asset
steps.description: For high-value or specialised equipment an outside appraiser gives orderly and forced liquidation values and the expected costs of sale, from a desktop review or a site visit.

evidence.note: Desktop appraisals 7 to 15 business days and on-site 15 to 25 business days, converted to calendar days.

steps.name: Decide on repairs and get quotes
steps.description: The specialist decides whether repairs would add more value than they cost, for example tires, batteries, a safety certificate for a truck, missing attachments or cleaning, and gets quotes from a dealer or repair shop.

error.defect_description: Repair approved that the market does not pay for.

evidence.note: BC PPSA s.59(2) allows disposal as is or after repair; the repair share is an author estimate.

steps.name: Approve the repair spend
steps.description: The manager of asset management and remarketing checks the quote against the expected price gain and the remaining balance or residual and approves spend above the specialist's limit or tells them to sell as is.

evidence.note: Author estimate.

steps.name: Repair shop reconditions the asset
steps.description: A dealer or repair shop does the approved work, which may include a provincial safety inspection for a truck or trailer, and invoices the company; the specialist checks the invoice against the quote.

evidence.note: Author estimate of shop turnaround.

steps.name: Choose the sales channel and set the reserve
steps.description: The specialist picks the channel: offer the asset back to the originating dealer or the dealer network, list it for a direct sale online, or consign it to a live or online auction, reserved or unreserved. The disposition plan records the reserve against the net book value or defaulted balance and the expected costs.

error.defect_description: Channel chosen that is slow for this equipment type.

evidence.note: Channel options follow the sources.

steps.name: Approve the disposition plan and minimum price
steps.description: The manager reviews the plan, checks that for seized equipment the notice of intended disposition period has run, that the sale method is commercially reasonable for the equipment and that the expected loss is within limits, and approves the channel and minimum price or asks for another plan.

control.basis: Provincial PPSA: notice before disposing of seized collateral (Ontario s.63(4), 15 days; BC s.59(6), 20 days) and a commercially reasonable sale (BC s.68(2)); company delegated authority for sale prices below book value

evidence.note: Channel split is an author estimate.

steps.name: Consign the asset to an auction
steps.description: The specialist signs the auction company's consignment contract on straight commission, chooses unreserved or reserved, sends the asset details, photos and serial numbers, confirms the company can give clear title and books the asset into the next suitable sale.

error.defect_description: Serial or description error on the listing.

evidence.note: Contract types and title checks follow the source; times are author estimates.

steps.name: Book transport to the auction yard
steps.description: The coordinator gets carrier quotes, issues the transport order and a release letter to the storage yard, and tracks the move; equipment sold through a weekly online auction can stay in the yard and skip this move.

error.defect_description: Wrong pickup site or missing release.

evidence.note: Online auctions sell from the seller's yard; times are author estimates.

steps.name: Asset moves and sells at the next auction
steps.description: The carrier moves the equipment, the auction company inspects and lists it, and it sells at the next weekly online auction or the next scheduled site auction.

evidence.note: Weekly online auctions on Thursdays in North America; site auctions are less frequent; the wait range is an author estimate.

steps.name: Auction company settles the proceeds
steps.description: After the buyer pays, the auction company sends the settlement statement with the hammer price, commission, fees and any charges, and wires the net proceeds. A reserved lot that does not meet its reserve comes back for a new plan.

next.condition: no sale at the reserve or buyer default

evidence.note: Settlement timing is an author estimate; the source says the auction company collects and disburses proceeds.

steps.name: Market the asset to dealers and buyers
steps.description: The specialist emails the asset to the originating dealer and a list of dealers who buy that equipment type, posts a listing with photos online, answers calls and arranges buyer inspections with the yard.

evidence.note: Dealer networks and private sales are named channels; times are author estimates.

steps.name: Buyers inspect and make offers
steps.description: Dealers and end buyers look at the photos or the equipment and send offers over the following weeks; some assets draw no acceptable offer and go back for a new plan, usually an auction.

evidence.note: Author estimate.

steps.name: Negotiate and accept the best offer
steps.description: The specialist compares the offers with the approved minimum price, negotiates with the best bidders and accepts an offer within the approval, or sends an offer below the minimum back to the manager.

evidence.note: Author estimate.

steps.name: Invoice the buyer with sales tax
steps.description: The specialist prepares the sale invoice and as-is, where-is terms with GST/HST and any provincial sales tax for the buyer's province, or records the dealer's resale exemption, and asks for a wire or certified funds before release.

error.defect_description: Wrong province or exemption, so tax is under-collected.

control.basis: Excise Tax Act s.183(2) (sale of seized property is a commercial activity) and GST/HST and provincial sales tax collection rules

evidence.note: Times are author estimates.

steps.name: Buyer pays for the asset
steps.description: The buyer wires the price or delivers certified funds; the specialist confirms the funds in the bank report before anything is released.

evidence.note: Author estimate.

steps.name: Release the asset to the buyer
steps.description: Once funds are confirmed the coordinator sends a release letter to the storage yard, agrees the pickup with the buyer's carrier and closes the storage account so daily charges stop.

error.defect_description: Storage not closed and charges keep running.

control.basis: Company policy: no release of equipment before cleared funds

evidence.note: Author estimate of common practice.

steps.name: Record the sale and apply the proceeds
steps.description: The specialist keys the gross price, commission, repair, transport and storage costs and the tax collected into the lease system from the settlement statement or invoice, closes the asset record, and applies the net proceeds to the defaulted contract or books the gain or loss against the residual on an off-lease asset.

error.defect_description: A cost or the tax split keyed wrongly.

evidence.note: Times and error rate are author estimates.

steps.name: Sign off the sale record
steps.description: The manager compares the sale price with the valuation and the approved minimum, checks the costs against invoices and the approvals on file, and signs the sale summary before month-end.

control.basis: Internal control: sales negotiated by one person are reviewed by another before the results are final

evidence.note: Author estimate of common practice.

steps.name: Post the sale journal and sales tax data
steps.description: The nightly interface posts the sale, costs, tax collected and gain or loss to the general ledger and loads the provincial tax amounts for the sales tax returns and the asset status for reporting.

evidence.note: Author estimate of the common interface set-up.

steps.name: Request the bill of sale and registration discharge
steps.description: The specialist sends lease administration the buyer's details, price and serial numbers so it can issue the bill of sale and discharge the company's personal property registration, which the buyer or auction company needs to show clear title.

error.defect_description: Wrong buyer name or serial on the request.

next.condition: seized equipment with a defaulted balance

evidence.note: A good-faith buyer takes free of the debtor's interest (s.59(14)); the split follows the trigger mix.

steps.name: Send the sale results to recoveries
steps.description: For seized equipment the specialist emails the recovery officer the settlement statement, net proceeds and all costs charged, so the deficiency can be calculated and the customer and guarantors told how the sale was done.

error.defect_description: A cost left off the summary.

evidence.note: Author estimate; the deficiency workflow (efc-recover-deficiencies-and-write-off) starts from this summary.

exceptions.name: Missing condition information
exceptions.description: The bailiff or return report lacks photos, hours or a function check, so an inspection is ordered before valuation.

exceptions.name: Third-party appraisal
exceptions.description: High-value or specialised equipment is appraised by an outside firm before the plan.

exceptions.name: Repairs before sale
exceptions.description: Repairs or a safety certificate are approved and done before marketing.

exceptions.name: No sale at the reserve
exceptions.description: A reserved auction lot does not sell or a direct listing draws no acceptable offer, and the asset is replanned, usually to an unreserved auction.

exceptions.name: Offer below the minimum
exceptions.description: The best direct offer is below the approved minimum and goes back to the manager.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from the asset entering remarketing inventory to sale recorded and results sent

evidence.note: Author estimate from weekly online and monthly site auction calendars, appraisal and repair turnaround and settlement after sale.

pain_points.description: Seized equipment often arrives with a thin bailiff report, so inspections and photos have to be ordered before anyone can price it.

evidence.note: Author estimate.

pain_points.description: Assets wait in paid storage for auction dates, repairs and settlements; storage charges and depreciation reduce the net recovery.

evidence.note: Depreciation and damage reduce amounts realised.

pain_points.description: Valuations depend on a few experienced asset managers checking auction results by hand.

evidence.note: Author estimate.

pain_points.description: Sale results are re-keyed from auction settlement statements and invoices into the lease system and then emailed to recoveries.

evidence.note: Author estimate.

sources.title: Ritchie Bros. Auctioneers Inc. annual report on Form 10-K for 2020
sources.supports: A majority of its auctions are unreserved; IronPlanet online auctions run every Thursday in North America; Marketplace-E offers reserve, make-offer and buy-now formats; straight commission, guarantee and inventory contracts, with guarantee and inventory about 20% of 2020 gross transaction value; title searches so equipment is sold free of liens; 2020 gross transaction value of $5.4 billion and commissions of $452.9 million (US dollars).

sources.title: Equipment appraisals
sources.supports: Lender appraisals give orderly liquidation, forced liquidation and fair market values, estimated liquidation costs and net recoverable value; desktop appraisals take 7 to 15 business days and on-site appraisals 15 to 25 business days.

sources.title: Personal Property Security Act [RSBC 1996] chapter 359
sources.supports: s.59(2): seized collateral may be disposed of as is or after repair; s.59(3): by private sale, public sale including auction or closed tender, whole or in parts; s.59(6): notice at least 20 days before disposition; s.59(14): a good-faith buyer takes free of the debtor's interest; s.68(2): rights must be exercised in good faith and in a commercially reasonable manner.

sources.title: Secured creditor must give reasonable notice before seizing defaulted assets: Court of Appeal
sources.supports: Ontario PPSA s.63(4) requires 15 days' notice before disposing of seized collateral; the exemption for goods customarily sold on a recognized market does not remove contractual and common law notice duties (1758704 Ontario Inc. v. Priest, 2021 ONCA 588).

sources.title: Excise Tax Act, section 183 (seizure and repossession)
sources.publisher: Justice Laws Website, Government of Canada
sources.supports: A creditor that seizes property is deemed to receive a supply at the time of seizure, and its later supply of the seized property is deemed made in the course of a commercial activity.

sources.title: Charter Equipment Lease 1998-1 LLC prospectus (Form 424B1)
sources.supports: The servicer uses commercially reasonable efforts to dispose of equipment on expiry or termination and may sell equipment of defaulted leases at public or private sale; depreciation, obsolescence and damage can leave sale proceeds below the amount due.

sources.title: The Collector Chronicles: beyond the default, how lenders master repossession and recovery
sources.supports: Seized equipment is liquidated through auctions, dealer networks or private sales; the sale must be commercially reasonable and a rushed or poorly marketed sale can be contested; agents document condition with photos.

assumptions: The auction_house trigger (remarketing_proceeds) arrives inside the case at step s15, so it has a share of zero; cases start when an asset enters remarketing inventory.
About 60% of sales are consigned to auctions and 40% sold to dealers or direct buyers; channel shares, reserves and approval limits are author estimates.
Consignment is listed with outcome 'any' because the format ties outputs to END outcomes, but only auction cases (about 60%) produce it.
The share of seized versus returned equipment (40/60) follows the organisation file's volumes for repossessions (about 45 a month) and off-lease returns (about 70 a month).
Notice of intended disposition is sent in the repossession process; this workflow only checks that the period has run before the sale.
Auction commission of about 8% is a whole-company average for one auction group; the company's own negotiated rates are not public.
External steps have no touch time; inspections, repairs, auctions and buyer payments are in wait_before_min.
Loaded costs are the organisation file's (2019-2022 wage times 1.35). Remarketing roles have no occupation code in the organisation file.
Legal rules named in controls are the author's reading of the cited statutes and reports, not legal advice.
